segments.text: Inside a modern tank, the crew sits in a steel box with a large amount of explosive, and
the designer's biggest decision was where to put it.
A single gun round weighs around 20 kilograms, a tank may carry 40 of them, and each one
contains a propellant charge that burns the way a firework does.
A hit that goes through the armor and finds that propellant can turn a 60-ton machine
into a fire in less than a second.
So a tank is, among many other things, a very careful arrangement of danger, with the crew
placed in whatever gaps are left.
So here is the question.
A tank is meant to be the strongest thing on a battlefield, yet every tank in history has
been destroyed by something smaller than itself.
What is it actually built to do, and what does it give up to do it?
The answer is a triangle of three things that cannot all be had together, plus a fourth
that decides who survives.
Each of the three can be improved only by taking from the others.
Start with firepower, the reason the thing exists.
Western tanks and most others carry a gun of 120 or 125 millimeters.
The shell that kills other tanks is not an explosive at all.
It is a long, thin dart of dense metal, fired at around one and a half cometers a second, which
punches through armor by sheer speed and concentrated weight, shoving a plug of metal and a spray
of fragments into the crew compartment.
The gun has to be accurate, and a tank can fire on the move because the barrel is stabilized,
so that a hull bouncing over fields does not move the aim.
Hitting is only half of it.
A gun that cannot see is useless, so the next layer is sight.
Modern tanks carry thermal cameras that see heat, so smoke and darkness stop being cover,
and a laser rangefinder that measures the distance in a blink, and a ballistic computer that turns
that number, plus wind and the temperature of the barrel, into the angle of the gun.
The crew does not aim in the way an old gunner did.
They put the mark on the target, press the laser, and the computer does the arithmetic.
The gunner has become a person who points and decides.
That was the offense.
The defense uses a lesson that was learned slowly.
Armor that is simply thick gets heavy fast, and a heavier tank cannot cross bridges or ride
a train, so modern armor is layered.
Plates of steel, ceramics, and other materials are bonded in sandwiches that blunt the dart,
and are built so that damaged sections can be replaced.
A large part of a tank's weight is armor, and most of that armor is on the front of the
turret and hull, where the enemy is expected to be.
It is thick where it is expected to be hit, and thin where it isn't.
There is a second kind of threat that armor has to answer, the shaped charge.
Rockets and many anti-tank missiles do not rely on speed.
They carry a hollow explosive cone, that on detonation, forms a narrow jet of metal moving
faster than the dart.
Thick plate is a poor defense against it, so tanks carry blocks of explosive on the
outside, called reactive armor, which detonate outward when hit and disturb the jet.
The armor fights back, and the trade is that it only works once for each block.
That choice has a price, which is the third corner, mobility.
A tank of 60 tons needs an engine of well over a thousand horsepower, and it drinks fuel
in a way that a car never would.
Some tanks use a gas turbine, the same family as a helicopter engine, which is powerful and
compact and very hungry.
Others use a diesel, which is slower to accelerate but goes much farther on a tank of fuel.
Neither is free.
A heavier tank is a thirstier one, and a thirstier tank needs more trucks behind it, which is
a problem the logistics of any army has to answer.
The tracks do a quiet job in all of this.
Spread across a long strip of rubber and steel, 60 tons presses on the ground with about the
pressure of a person standing, which is why a tank can cross a muddy field that would swallow
a truck.
The price is noise, wear, and a track that can break.
A thrown track is the most common way a tank stops without being shot at, and a crew that
cannot repair it in the open becomes a target.
Weight also sets limits far from the battlefield.
A 60-ton vehicle breaks light bridges and soft roads, and an army with heavy tanks needs transporters
and bridge layers to move them, which takes us back to the logistics chain.
A lighter tank can go more places and can be carried by a few aircraft.
A heavier one can survive more but moves less.
Designers often accept the heavier one, because a tank that arrives and is destroyed is worth
less than a tank that arrives and endures.
All of that sits inside a hull with very little space, which is the fourth thing that decides
the rest.
Everything has to fit.
The guns breach, the ammunition, the engine, the crew, the sights, the radios.
The crew of three or four sits in a space smaller than a van.
The human body has to reach the controls, reload the gun, breathe in the fumes of firing,
and be shielded from the shock of a hit.
Squeezing the volume lets the designer cover it with thicker armor per ton, so every cubic
meter saved is worth tons of protection.
This is why the choice of loader matters.
Some tanks use a person to load each round, which needs space, a fourth crew member, and
a lot of effort in a pitching hull.
Others use an autoloader, a mechanism that picks a round from a carousel and puts it in
the breech.
That saves a person and makes the tank lower and smaller, which is attractive.
The trade is where the ammunition sits.
In some designs, the rounds are stored in a ring around the floor of the crew compartment,
and a hit there can set them all off, sometimes throwing the turret into the air.
In others, the ammunition is kept in a separate compartment at the back of the turret with
panels that blow outward, so that the force escapes the crew.
There is a small joke in that.
Tank designers are among the few engineers whose best result is a vehicle that looks fine
from the outside while being wrecked inside, because the blow-off panel did exactly what
it was built for, and the crew walked away from the burnt-out turret.
A tank that is destroyed and a tank that has been survived can look identical to anyone who
is not inside it.
Even the turret is a piece of trickery.
Because the gun is in a rotating turret, the tank can park behind a ridge, with only
the top of the turret showing, which is called being hauled down, and fire while the thickest
and most expensive part of the vehicle stays hidden.
A gun that can depress below the horizontal makes the trick work on a reverse slope.
The vehicle shows a few square meters to the enemy and holds the rest in reserve.
Much of tank design is about showing the enemy less of what is weak.
Then there is the last part of the story.
For most of the 20th century, the tank was threatened from the front, and its armor was built for
that.
Today, many of the dangers come from above.
A drone dropping a small charge onto the thin roof of the turret, or a missile that flies
over the target and then dives, does not meet the heavy armor at all.
It strikes the one place where there is little of it, because covering the top with the same
plate would double the weight.
So tanks have grown cages and nets and sensors, which were once thought of as clumsy, and the
crews watch the sky as well as the ground.
There is also the matter of what a crew cannot see.
Sealed inside, with the hatches closed, they look at the world through narrow periscopes
and a screen, and a tank in a town or a wood is nearly blind to anyone close to it.
A soldier with a short-range rocket can sit in a window and be invisible.
This is why tanks move with infantry, who watch the places the crew cannot, while the tank takes
the fire that would otherwise land on them.
Each protects the other from its own blind spots.
Which is what makes the tank so hard to judge from outside.
A tank is not strong because it can survive being hit.
It is strong because it is rarely hit, because it moves between cover, because it fires first,
and because infantry, artillery, and drones around it find the threats before they find the tank.
That is my own reading, but it suggests that armor is the last line of the defense and not
the first.
A tank alone is a target, a tank in a system is a weapon.
So return to the box full of explosive and the four people in it.
Every part, the gun, the sights, the layers of armor, the engine, the carousel, and the
blow-off panel, answers the same question, which is how to bring far more energy to a fight
than a person could ever carry and leave the person alive when it arrives.
A tank is not a monument to strength.
It is a very careful negotiation.
